chapter_title: FPGA Interfacing: GPIO, UART, SPI, Memory, and Analog
chapter_summary:
FPGAs are powerful because they can interface with a wide variety of external devices. Unlike microcontrollers, which have fixed peripheral sets, FPGAs can implement any interface protocol in hardware, allowing you to connect to custom sensors, legacy devices, and high-speed peripherals. This chapter covers the most common interfaces used in FPGA-based embedded systems.

**GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output):** GPIO is the simplest interface. FPGA pins can be configured as inputs or outputs, and you can read or write them directly from your HDL code. The DE10-Lite board has 8 LEDs and 2 pushbuttons connected to GPIO pins. A GPIO controller in Verilog is just a register connected to the I/O pins:

```verilog
module gpio_controller (
    input  wire        clk,
    input  wire        wr_en,
    input  wire [7:0]  wr_data,
    output reg  [7:0]  gpio_out,
    input  wire [1:0]  gpio_in,
    output reg  [1:0]  gpio_in_reg
);
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (wr_en)
            gpio_out <= wr_data;
        gpio_in_reg <= gpio_in;
    end
endmodule
```

**UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter):** UART is a serial communication protocol used for debugging, GPS modules, Bluetooth modules, and PC communication. A UART controller in Verilog consists of a baud rate generator, a transmitter shift register, and a receiver shift register. The transmitter serializes parallel data by shifting it out one bit at a time. The receiver deserializes incoming serial data by sampling the input at the baud rate. A typical UART frame is: start bit (0), 8 data bits, optional parity bit, and 1 or 2 stop bits (1).

```verilog
module uart_tx (
    input  wire        clk,
    input  wire        tx_start,
    input  wire [7:0]  tx_data,
    output reg         tx_busy,
    output reg         tx_serial
);
    // Baud rate counter and shift register logic
    // ... (implementation details)
endmodule
```

**SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface):** SPI is a synchronous serial protocol used for flash memory, SD cards, displays, and sensors. It has four signals: SCLK (clock), MOSI (master out, slave in), MISO (master in, slave out), and CS (chip select). An SPI master controller in Verilog generates the clock and shifts data in and out. SPI is faster than UART and supports full-duplex communication.

**I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit):** I2C is a two-wire synchronous serial protocol (SDA for data, SCL for clock) used for sensors, EEPROMs, and real-time clocks. It is slower than SPI but uses fewer wires and supports multiple masters and slaves on the same bus. An I2C controller in Verilog must implement start/stop condition detection, bit-level arbitration, and acknowledge bit handling. I2C is more complex to implement in hardware than SPI because of the open-drain bus and arbitration.

**Memory Interfaces:**
- **On-chip BRAM:** FPGA Block RAM (BRAM) provides fast, dedicated memory. A dual-port BRAM can be read and written simultaneously from two different clock domains. In Verilog, BRAM is inferred by describing a memory array with clocked read and write operations:

```verilog
reg [7:0] memory [0:1023];  // 1K x 8 RAM

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (we)
        memory[addr] <= wr_data;
    rd_data <= memory[addr];
end
```

- **External SDRAM:** The DE10-Lite board has 64 MB of external SDRAM. Accessing SDRAM requires a memory controller that handles refresh cycles, row/column addressing, and burst transfers. Fortunately, the Quartus Prime IP Catalog provides a ready-to-use SDRAM controller that connects to the NIOS II processor via the Avalon bus.

**Analog Interfaces:**
The Intel MAX 10 FPGA has a built-in **12-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC)** with up to 18 channels. This is a unique feature of the MAX 10 that makes it ideal for sensor-based applications. The ADC can be accessed through the Quartus Prime IP Catalog or directly from the NIOS II processor using the ADC IP core. The ADC supports single-ended and differential inputs, programmable sample rates, and internal temperature sensing.

To use the ADC:
1. Add the ADC IP core to your Qsys system.
2. Configure the sample rate and input channels.
3. Connect the ADC to the NIOS II processor via the Avalon bus.
4. In software, read the ADC value using the HAL API:

```c
alt_u32 adc_value = IORD(ADC_BASE, 0);  // Read channel 0
float voltage = (adc_value / 4095.0) * 3.3;  // Convert to voltage
```

This allows the FPGA to acquire analog signals from sensors, potentiometers, or microphones without any external ADC chip.

screens.title: FPGA Interfacing: GPIO, UART, SPI, Memory & ADC
screens.subtitle: Practical hardware interfaces and Verilog patterns for embedded FPGA systems

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to connect real-world devices to an FPGA and why flexible hardware interfaces matter. We start with the simplest building block, general purpose input and output, showing how an FPGA pin becomes an input or output in your Verilog. Then we move to serial links: UART for simple text and debugging, and SPI for higher-speed, full-duplex transfers. You will also see I2C’s tradeoffs and why it is more complex to implement in fabric. Memory is next: how on-chip BRAM gives fast, local storage and how external SDRAM is handled through a controller IP that manages refresh and bursts. Finally, we examine the Intel MAX 10 embedded ADC and how it lets your design sample analog sensors without extra chips. Each topic includes Verilog examples, a demonstration idea to test on a DE10-Lite board, and a small verification checklist. By the end you’ll know how to pick the right interface for a sensor or peripheral, write the needed HDL modules, and validate them with a testbench. Which physical signal do you need to expose first on your next prototype?

keyIdea.title: Why interfacing matters
keyIdea.text: FPGAs can implement almost any peripheral in hardware, letting you connect custom sensors and high-speed devices. Choosing the right interface and verifying it in HDL is essential for reliable embedded systems.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives break the chapter into usable skills you can apply immediately. First, you will learn to interface external devices using GPIO, UART, SPI, and I2C. That means understanding signal direction, timing, and basic Verilog registers to drive pins and sample inputs. Second, you will implement memory interfaces: infer BRAM in your RTL for fast local storage and connect external SDRAM using a controller from Quartus’ IP catalog. Third, you’ll use the Intel MAX 10 embedded ADC to capture analog sensor data and convert raw counts into voltages inside software running on the NIOS II. Finally, you will write Verilog modules for protocol controllers and verify them with testbenches: this includes building a UART transmitter and receiver, verifying start and stop bit timing, and simulating an SPI transaction. Each objective is hands-on. For example, you’ll toggle DE10-Lite LEDs with a GPIO register, observe UART frames on a logic analyzer, and read an ADC channel into a variable. These skills let you choose the right interface and prove it works before deploying into hardware.

keyIdea.title: Skill-focused objectives
keyIdea.text: Translate interface requirements into Verilog modules, select memory strategies, and validate behavior with simulation and simple hardware checks.

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on actionable verification and system integration. You will write Verilog protocol controllers and create testbenches that verify timing and correctness. A concrete skill is building a UART echo: transmit and receive bytes at 115200 baud on a 50 megahertz clock and confirm timing with simulation. You will also learn how to configure ADC sampling and convert raw counts to voltages in software, including the conversion formula used on a 12-bit ADC with a 3.3 volt reference. Another objective is integrating BRAM and SDRAM into a system: infer an M9K-like block from RTL for small buffers, and connect a Quartus SDRAM IP to the NIOS II via Avalon for larger memory. Lastly, you will practice debugging hardware with simple experiments: toggle LEDs for GPIO checks, capture UART frames on a logic analyzer, or read ADC values while changing a potentiometer. These activities make sure designs are not only syntactically correct but also functionally verified on board.

screens.title: GPIO: Pins, Registers, and a Simple Verilog Controller
screens.subtitle: How FPGA pins become read/write registers in your design

narration.text: GPIO is the simplest and most immediate interface to external hardware. At its core, a GPIO controller maps physical pins to registers in your HDL so your design can read switches or drive LEDs. The example controller in the chapter shows exactly that: a write enable that updates an output register and a sampled input register for buttons. When you write this in Verilog, the behavioral description synthesis infers the proper pin connections and registers. A concrete example is the DE10-Lite board which exposes 8 LEDs and 2 pushbuttons: a small controller writes an 8-bit pattern to the LEDs and samples the buttons each clock cycle. A common misconception is to treat GPIO as slow or secondary; in fact, using clocked registers and careful synchronization makes GPIO reliable and debounced when needed. If you sample asynchronous inputs, you must add sync stages to avoid metastability—this is often missed by beginners. Key takeaway: start with a clear register interface in Verilog, connect to the board pin assignments, and verify with simple hardware checks. Try toggling LEDs from your register and observing the result — does the observed behavior match your written register at the clock edges?

keyIdea.title: GPIO maps directly to registers
keyIdea.text: A small Verilog controller converts pins to readable or writable registers; synchronize asynchronous inputs to avoid metastability.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.1 › GPIO
GPIO Controller in Verilog
Register mapping example and synchronization note.
Verilog Example
<!-- Verilog: gpio_controller -->
module gpio_controller (
  input  wire        clk,
  input  wire        wr_en,
  input  wire [7:0]  wr_data,
  output reg  [7:0]  gpio_out,
  input  wire [1:0]  gpio_in,
  output reg  [1:0]  gpio_in_reg
);
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (wr_en)
      gpio_out <= wr_data;
    gpio_in_reg <= gpio_in;
  end
endmodule
Explanation
  • gpio_out stores the 8-bit LED pattern when wr_en is asserted.
  • gpio_in_reg samples asynchronous buttons at clock edges; add extra sync registers on noisy inputs.
  • Map these signals to board pin constraints in the .qsf or pin planner.
Concrete Example
On DE10-Lite, write 0xFF to gpio_out to light all 8 LEDs. Press a button and observe gpio_in_reg update in simulation before hardware check.
Key Takeaway

GPIO is simple but requires clocked sampling and synchronization for reliable input handling.

screens.title: UART Internals: Baud, Shift Registers, and Framing
screens.subtitle: How a UART transmitter and receiver work in Verilog

narration.text: UART is a byte-oriented asynchronous serial protocol used widely for debugging and simple peripheral links. A UART controller typically includes a baud rate generator, a transmitter shift register, and a receiver shift register. The transmitter loads parallel data, appends frame bits, and shifts them out at the baud clock. The receiver samples the line at the baud timing, detects the start bit, reads the data bits, and checks stop bits. A practical example is sending an ASCII character from a PC through a USB-to-UART bridge to the FPGA; the FPGA receives the framed bits, reconstructs the byte, and can echo it back. A common misconception is that UART must be high speed to be useful — in fact, reliability depends on stable baud timing and sampling at the correct edges. If you compute a baud counter for 115200 bps with a 50 MHz clock, you must ensure the counter increments precisely and that sampling aligns with the middle of each bit. In verification, assert that start bit timing and stop bit presence are respected. Try simulating a transmitter module to watch the serialized bits and confirm the framing is correct. What observable evidence will prove your UART is sampling in the middle of each bit?

keyIdea.title: UART frames are timed, not packetized
keyIdea.text: Transmitters serialize bytes and receivers must sample at correct baud timing; timing alignment is the key to reliable UART links.

content.html:
Module 9 › UART
UART: transmitter & receiver
Baud generator plus shift registers form a UART controller.
Module Sketch
<!-- Verilog: uart_tx skeleton -->
module uart_tx (
  input  wire        clk,
  input  wire        tx_start,
  input  wire [7:0]  tx_data,
  output reg         tx_busy,
  output reg         tx_serial
);
  // Baud rate counter and shift register logic
  // load tx_data, append stop bit, shift out at baud clock
endmodule
What to verify
  • Start bit is logic 0 and spans one full baud period.
  • Each data bit is sampled at the baud mid-point for stability.
  • Stop bit is logic 1; missing stop bits indicate framing errors.
Concrete Example
Connect FPGA UART to a PC terminal. Send an ASCII character from the PC. The FPGA should receive the frame, reconstruct the byte, and optionally echo it back.
Common Mistake

Miscalculating the baud divider causes bit drift and framing errors. Always verify divider math for your clock domain.

screens.title: SPI vs I2C: When to choose which bus
screens.subtitle: Tradeoffs in wires, speed, and arbitration

narration.text: SPI and I2C are two common synchronous serial buses with different strengths. SPI uses four signals — clock, MOSI, MISO, and chip select — enabling full-duplex transfers and higher practical clock rates. It’s an excellent choice for flash memory, SD cards, displays, and fast sensors where point-to-point communication is acceptable. I2C uses two lines, data and clock, with open-drain drivers and pull-ups. That makes I2C simpler in wiring and suitable for multiple devices on a shared bus, but it also requires start/stop condition handling, acknowledge bits, and arbitration logic for multi-master cases. Implementing I2C in HDL is more complex because you must emulate open-drain behavior and detect bus collisions. A concrete example: an SPI master can shift out a command to a flash chip while simultaneously reading returned data on MISO; this full-duplex flow is hard to replicate on I2C. A common misconception is that I2C is always slower; while often true, I2C speed depends on pull-up sizing and bus capacitance. Key takeaway: pick SPI when you need speed and simplicity of master-slave links, pick I2C when you need many low-pin-count devices and built-in addressing.

keyIdea.title: Bus choice matters
keyIdea.text: SPI for speed and full-duplex point-to-point links; I2C for shared, low-pin-count multi-device buses despite added arbitration complexity.

content.html:
Module 9 › SPI & I2C
SPI vs I2C
Compare wires, timing, and implementation complexity.
SPI — Key Points
  • Signals: SCLK, MOSI, MISO, CS.
  • Full duplex; master controls clock and chip select.
  • Simpler HDL: generate clock edges and shift registers.
Example: Read flash memory with a burst transfer while SCLK toggles at high frequency.
I2C — Key Points
  • Signals: SDA and SCL with open-drain drivers and pull-ups.
  • Supports multiple masters and slaves with addressing and ACK bits.
  • HDL must implement start/stop detection and arbitration handling.
Common Mistake: forgetting to model open-drain behavior or neglecting bus capacitance effects on speed.
Choose SPI
Fast, full-duplex transfers for flash and sensors.
Choose I2C
Multiple low-pin-count devices, slower but flexible bus.
Key Takeaway

Match the bus to the device’s speed, wiring constraints, and multi-device requirements before writing HDL.

screens.title: BRAM Inference in Verilog
screens.subtitle: Describing on-chip memory and the synthesizer's role

narration.text: FPGA block R A M, often called BRAM or M9K/M10K depending on the family, is inferred from memory-like RTL descriptions. The typical pattern is a reg array indexed by an address and clocked read/write operations. A dual-port BRAM allows two independent accesses, which is useful for simultaneous read and write from different clock domains or ports. The chapter shows an 8-bit by 1K example that synthesizes to on-chip R A M when the tool recognizes the pattern. A concrete example is using BRAM to hold a small lookup table or buffer that needs low latency. Beginners sometimes think BRAM must be instantiated from a vendor primitive directly; while you can instantiate vendor R A M macros, modern synthesis will infer BRAM from simple array patterns which is clearer and more portable. When you infer R A M, check RTL Viewer or synthesis reports to confirm the tool mapped your array to an M9K or equivalent block. Key takeaway: write clear, clocked memory descriptions and inspect the synthesis report to ensure the intended physical block is used. BRAM Inference in Verilog means describe memory as clocked arrays in verilog; synthesis infers bram, giving faster local storage without manual instantiation.. In practical terms, describing on-chip memory and the synthesizer's role. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Infer BRAM from arrays
keyIdea.text: Describe memory as clocked arrays in Verilog; synthesis infers BRAM, giving faster local storage without manual instantiation.

content.html:
Module 9 › BRAM
BRAM Inference
Describe memory behavior in RTL and let the synthesizer infer block RAM.
Verilog Pattern
reg [7:0] memory [0:1023];  // 1K x 8 RAM

always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (we)
    memory[addr] <= wr_data;
  rd_data <= memory[addr];
end
Explanation
A clocked array with conditional writes is the canonical pattern that synthesis tools detect and map to BRAM blocks. Use separate read or registered read styles depending on latency needs.
Concrete Example
Use a 1K x 8 BRAM as a small packet FIFO or coefficient table. Validate via RTL Viewer to ensure an M9K/M10K block is used.
Key Takeaway

Describe behavior clearly in RTL and confirm the synthesizer’s mapping to the expected physical memory block.

screens.title: External SDRAM: Controller IP and System Integration
screens.subtitle: Why use an IP controller and how it connects to processors

narration.text: Unlike BRAM, external SDRAM requires careful control of refresh cycles, row/column addressing, and burst transfers, which is why FPGA projects typically use a vendor-provided SDRAM controller IP. The Quartus Prime IP Catalog provides an SDRAM controller that handles low-level timing and exposes a higher-level bus interface such as Avalon. In practice, you connect the SDRAM controller to a soft processor like NIOS II so software can read and write large data buffers. A concrete example from the chapter: the DE10-Lite’s 64 megabyte SDRAM is accessed via the controller and Avalon bridge, which automatically schedules refreshes and burst reads. A common misconception is that you should write your own SDRAM controller for every project; in most cases, using the vendor IP saves development time and reduces timing bugs. When integrating, validate that the controller’s pin assignments match the board DDR layout and that the timing constraints are applied in the project. Key takeaway: prefer proven SDRAM IP for reliable external memory access and focus your efforts on system-level integration and software testing rather than reinventing refresh logic. External SDRAM: Controller IP and System Integration means sdram needs refresh and complex timing; vendor ip exposes a clean bus interface and frees you to focus on system integration.. In practical terms, why use an ip controller and how it connects to processors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use controller IP for SDRAM
keyIdea.text: SDRAM needs refresh and complex timing; vendor IP exposes a clean bus interface and frees you to focus on system integration.

content.html:
Module 9 › SDRAM
External SDRAM via IP
Connect controller IP to processor buses for large off-chip memory.
Architecture Overview
  • SDRAM controller handles refresh, row/column commands, and burst transfers.
  • Expose an Avalon or similar bus to the processor for easy reads/writes.
  • Check timing constraints and pin mapping against board documentation.
Concrete Example
Use Quartus SDRAM IP to connect the DE10-Lite 64 MB SDRAM to NIOS II. Perform a simple DMA or burst read to move large buffers between SDRAM and BRAM-backed peripherals.
Integration Checklist
  • Match SDRAM timing parameters in IP configuration.
  • Assign pins as the board schematic requires.
  • Run a memory test from software to confirm read/write and burst behavior.
Key Takeaway

Rely on proven SDRAM IP and validate the integration with software memory tests rather than reimplementing low-level timing logic.

screens.title: Intel MAX 10 ADC: Configuration and Reading Values
screens.subtitle: Access the built-in 12-bit ADC and convert counts to voltage

narration.text: The Intel MAX 10 FPGA includes a 12-bit ADC with multiple channels, a valuable feature for sensor-based systems because it removes the need for an external ADC chip. Accessing the ADC often uses the Quartus IP and an Avalon connection to a processor like NIOS II. The chapter details the steps: add the ADC IP core, configure sample rate and channels, connect to the Avalon bus, and read samples from software. A practical code example shows reading the ADC register and converting the 12-bit count into voltage using the formula that divides by 4095 and multiplies by the 3.3 volt reference. For instance, reading a raw value and computing voltage in C with the HAL A P I yields a numeric voltage that you can log or use in control logic. A misconception to watch for is assuming ADC values are equal to voltages — you must perform the conversion taking into account resolution and reference. Also, confirm whether single-ended or differential inputs are being used and set channel configuration accordingly. Key takeaway: use the ADC IP and simple software conversion to bring analog sensor readings into your embedded application.

keyIdea.title: ADC brings analog into digital
keyIdea.text: Use the MAX 10 ADC IP and a simple conversion in software to turn 12-bit counts into voltages for sensor processing.

content.html:
Module 9 › ADC
MAX 10 Embedded ADC
IP configuration and reading values in software.
C Software Example
alt_u32 adc_value = IORD(ADC_BASE, 0);  // Read channel 0
float voltage = (adc_value / 4095.0) * 3.3;  // Convert to voltage
Explanation
The ADC returns a 12-bit count. Divide by 4095.0 to get a normalized value, then multiply by the reference voltage to obtain the measured voltage.
Concrete Example
If adc_value is 2048 on a 3.3V reference, the computed voltage is about 1.65 volts. Use this to calibrate sensors or drive decisions in your logic or software.
Key Takeaway

Configure the ADC IP, read channel counts, and convert to voltage in software. Confirm single-ended/differential modes for correct wiring.

screens.title: Writing and Verifying Verilog Protocol Controllers
screens.subtitle: From module design to testbench verification and board check

narration.text: A reliable development flow starts with a clear module interface, proceeds through simulation-based verification, and finishes with simple hardware checks on the board. When you write a protocol controller such as UART or SPI, begin by defining clock domains, input and output signals, and control flags like start or busy. Implement the core behavior—shift registers for serial data, baud counters for timing, and state machines for command sequences. Then write a testbench that drives stimulus vectors mimicking bus activity: for UART, simulate a serial line with a correctly timed start bit and data bits; for SPI, toggle chip select and provide MOSI data while observing MISO. The chapter’s hands-on activity asks you to implement a UART controller at 115200 baud with a 50 MHz clock and verify timing of start, data, and stop bits. After simulation, synthesize and program the DE10-Lite board. Validate by sending a character from a PC over USB-to-UART and observing an echo, and optionally examine waveforms on a logic analyzer or oscilloscope. A frequent misconception is skipping unit tests for corner cases such as framing errors or arbitration outcomes; exhaustive test vectors save time on hardware debugging. Key takeaway: simulation-first development plus small, focused hardware checks ensures correctness before system integration.

keyIdea.title: Simulate then test on board
keyIdea.text: Design modules with clear interfaces, verify timing in a testbench, then confirm behavior with small hardware experiments like UART echo.

content.html:
Module 9 › Verification
Design → Testbench → Hardware
A minimal verification flow for protocol controllers.
Step-by-step
  1. Define module interface and clock domain.
  2. Implement logic: shift registers, counters, state machines.
  3. Write testbench with edge timing checks and error cases.
  4. Synthesize and run a small on-board test like UART echo.
Concrete Lab
Implement UART at 115200 baud with a 50 MHz clock. Write a testbench verifying bit timing then program DE10-Lite and confirm echo via PC terminal.
Common Mistake
Neglecting edge cases like framing errors or simultaneous accesses. Add test vectors to cover these scenarios early.
Key Takeaway

A disciplined testbench and a small in-hardware check reduce debugging time and increase confidence in your controller modules.

screens.title: System Integration: Putting GPIO, UART, Memory, and ADC Together
screens.subtitle: A simple architecture that ties peripherals to a processor or state machine

narration.text: Real embedded FPGA projects combine peripherals into a cohesive system. One common pattern is a lightweight state machine or soft processor that accesses: GPIO for simple control and status, UART for debug or command input and output, BRAM for low-latency buffers, SDRAM for large datasets, and the MAX 10 ADC for sensor inputs. Architecturally, the SDRAM controller sits as a memory slave connected to the Avalon bus, BRAM provides fast local storage, and peripherals expose registers the processor reads and writes. A concrete scenario: a data acquisition design samples an analog input through the ADC, stores samples in BRAM for immediate processing, and flushes larger blocks to SDRAM via DMA. Commands and monitoring use UART so a PC can request samples or change parameters. A frequent misconception is assuming all components share timing requirements; in practice, separate clock domains and clock crossing synchronization are often necessary. Key takeaway: design clear interfaces and data paths between subsystems, plan for clock domain crossings, and validate each link with targeted tests before full-system runs. System Integration: Putting GPIO, UART, Memory, and ADC Together means map sensors and memories into a system bus or well-defined state machine, and handle clock domain crossings and buffering explicitly.. In practical terms, a simple architecture that ties peripherals to a processor or state machine. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design clear data paths
keyIdea.text: Map sensors and memories into a system bus or well-defined state machine, and handle clock domain crossings and buffering explicitly.

content.html:
Module 9 › Integration
System Integration Pattern
A minimal architecture tying peripherals to a bus or control logic.
Hierarchy
Processor or controller core
  • Access registers exposed by GPIO, UART, ADC.
  • Perform DMA to BRAM or SDRAM for bulk transfers.
Concrete Scenario
Sample analog via ADC, store immediate samples in BRAM for processing, and move larger buffers to SDRAM for logging. Use UART for commands and result reporting.
Clock Domain Note
If ADC, core, and external memory run on different clocks, add synchronization or FIFOs at domain boundaries to prevent data loss or metastability.
Key Takeaway

Plan interfaces and buffering around clock domains and the expected data rates for each peripheral when integrating a system.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas to carry forward. First, GPIO maps pins to registers in HDL; synchronize inputs to prevent metastability and use simple controllers for immediate hardware feedback. Second, UART is an asynchronous framed protocol that depends on accurate baud timing; implement baud generators and sample in the bit center to avoid framing errors. Third, SPI provides full-duplex, high-speed transfers with dedicated clock and chip select lines, while I2C trades speed for fewer wires and requires open-drain arbitration logic. Each of these choices influences HDL complexity and wiring on your board. Remember these core concepts as you design or choose interfaces for sensors and peripherals. Key Concepts means map signals to registers, respect timing, and choose the right bus for speed and wiring constraints.. In practical terms, what to remember from this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Key Concepts
Key Concepts
Three compact reminders of what matters.
GPIO Controller
Pins are registers; use clocked updates and input synchronization for reliability.
UART & SPI
UART needs correct baud sampling; SPI offers full-duplex with dedicated clock and chip select lines.
BRAM & SDRAM
Infer BRAM from RTL arrays; use vendor SDRAM IP for refresh and burst transfers.
Takeaway

Choose the right interface for your device, verify timing in simulation, and confirm behavior with small hardware tests.

narration.text: A few practical checks will save time. Always inspect synthesis or RTL Viewer to confirm BRAM inference; verify baud divider math for UART to avoid drifting frames; ensure SPI signals include chip select to delimit transactions; implement open-drain behavior and arbitration detection for I2C; and confirm ADC channel modes and reference voltage when converting counts to volts. The hands-on lab reinforces these checks: implement and test a UART echo at 115200 baud using a 50 megahertz clock, run simulations that check start and stop bit timing, and use simple LED toggles or a logic analyzer to observe the real signals on the DE10-Lite. These concrete verifications turn HDL descriptions into dependable hardware behavior. What small test will you run first on your board? content.html:
Module 9 › Final Notes
What to Remember
Simple checks and tests that prevent common errors.
Check Synthesis
Confirm BRAM inference and block usage in the RTL Viewer or synthesis report.
Verify Timing
Compute baud dividers and run timing checks; simulate framing and burst timing for memory interfaces.
Test on Board
Start with LED toggles, UART echo, ADC read with a potentiometer, and simple memory reads to confirm end-to-end behavior.
Final Takeaway

Small, repeatable tests and careful verification are the fastest route from HDL prototypes to reliable FPGA systems.
